content: These guidelines aim to support national TB control programs, policymakers, and healthcare providers in diverse settings by offering updated recommendations based on the latest evidence. The guidelines were developed by a multidisciplinary Guideline Development Group (GDG) convened by WHO's Global TB Programme. This group included TB experts, national TB program managers, civil society representatives, and academic researchers. The GDG reviewed evidence on key aspects of TB treatment and patient care, including the effectiveness of treatment regimens, adherence interventions, and models of care. The recommendations were formulated using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach, except in cases where evidence was insufficient, in which case a good practice statement was used. Key recommendations include: 1. Treatment Regimens: A 6-month rifampicin-based regimen (2HRZE/4HR) remains the standard treatment for drug-susceptible pulmonary TB. Shortened 4-month fluoroquinolone-containing regimens are not recommended (strong recommendation, moderate certainty in evidence). Fixed-dose combination (FDC) tablets are recommended over separate drug formulations for TB treatment (conditional recommendation, low certainty in evidence). Daily dosing of TB medications is recommended over intermittent (thrice-weekly) dosing during both the intensive and continuation phases of treatment (conditional recommendation, very low certainty in evidence). 2. TB and HIV Co-Infection: Antiretroviral therapy (ART) should be initiated in all TB patients living with HIV, regardless of CD4 cell count (strong recommendation, high certainty in evidence). TB treatment should be started first, followed by ART within the first 8 weeks of TB treatment. For patients with CD4 counts below 50 cells/mm³, ART should be initiated within the first 2 weeks of TB treatment. 3. Adjuvant Corticosteroid Therapy: In patients with tuberculous meningitis, initial adjuvant corticosteroid therapy with dexamethasone or prednisolone tapered over 6–8 weeks is recommended (strong recommendation, moderate certainty in evidence). In patients with tuberculous pericarditis, adjuvant corticosteroid therapy may be used (conditional recommendation, very low certainty in evidence). 4. Retreatment of TB: The WHO Category II regimen should no longer be used for patients requiring TB retreatment. Instead, drug-susceptibility testing should guide the choice of treatment regimen (good practice statement). 5. Patient Care and Adherence: Health education and counseling on TB disease and treatment adherence should be provided to all patients on TB treatment (strong recommendation, moderate certainty in evidence). A package of treatment adherence interventions, such as SMS reminders, medication monitors, or psychological support, may be offered based on individual patient needs and available resources (conditional recommendation, low to moderate certainty in evidence). Communityor home-based directly observed treatment (DOT) is recommended over health facility-based DOT or unsupervised treatment (conditional recommendation, moderate certainty in evidence). Video-observed treatment (VOT) can replace DOT when video communication technology is available and can be appropriately organized (conditional recommendation, very low certainty in evidence). The guidelines emphasize the importance of individualized care, patient-centered approaches, and the use of evidence-based interventions to improve treatment outcomes. WHO also highlights the need for ongoing research to address gaps in evidence and improve TB care globally.
